quests.instruction: Which form has the full ending typical of British English?
quests.hint: You have met this ending in missile and fragile. What does the last syllable sound like here?
quests.explanation: British English commonly says /ˈfjuːtaɪl/. American English reduces the ending to /ˈfjuːtl/.
quests.dialectNote: Word families let you generalise: the same suffix behaves alike in several words.

quests.instruction: Which form is more typical of American English?
quests.hint: Focus on the last syllable and compare its vowel.
quests.explanation: American /ˈstɛrəl/ has a weak final syllable. British /ˈsteraɪl/ ends in a full diphthong.
quests.dialectNote: Medical vocabulary often contains this suffix.

quests.instruction: Which version might you hear in a British workplace?
quests.hint: Project teams use this word often, so this is a useful test.
quests.explanation: British /ˈædʒaɪl/ keeps the full vowel; American often has /ˈædʒəl/.
quests.dialectNote: The pattern isn't absolute: some American speakers use the full ending.

quests.instruction: Which form suits General American?
quests.hint: This noun begins with the same syllable as 'process' but does the vowel follow the same pattern?
quests.explanation: American /ˈprɑːɡrɛs/ has an unrounded first vowel; British /ˈprəʊɡres/ has a diphthong.
quests.dialectNote: The pro- pattern is shared by process, progress, project, product.

quests.instruction: Which form is British?
quests.hint: The first vowel is again the point. Ask whether it is rounded.
quests.explanation: British /ˈprɒdʒekt/ has a rounded /ɒ/. American /ˈprɑːdʒekt/ has /ɑː/.
quests.dialectNote: The noun and verb forms differ in stress, but not in this vowel.

quests.instruction: Which form would many Southern British speakers use?
quests.hint: This is a business word that appears in many meetings.
quests.explanation: British /ˈprɒdʌkt/ has /ɒ/; American /ˈprɑːdʌkt/ has /ɑː/.
quests.dialectNote: Once you know the pattern, several words become easy.

quests.instruction: Which form matches Southern British English?
quests.hint: In this word the vowel is followed by a single consonant, unlike in 'dance'.
quests.explanation: Banana is one of the words with /ɑː/ in Southern British (/bəˈnɑːnə/) even without a consonant cluster.
quests.dialectNote: This shows that some words are exceptions to the cluster rule.

quests.instruction: Which version is common in Southern British English?
quests.hint: The spelling differs across the Atlantic (pyjamas / pajamas). Does the vowel also differ?
quests.explanation: British /pəˈdʒɑːməz/ has a long vowel; American /pəˈdʒæməz/ has a short one.
quests.dialectNote: Spelling and pronunciation differences often go together.

quests.instruction: Which version is typical of General American?
quests.hint: This is an interesting reversal. The loanword behaves the opposite way.
quests.explanation: In American English, pasta usually has /ɑː/, /ˈpɑːstə/. British English has /ˈpæstə/.
quests.dialectNote: Italian loanwords follow their own patterns, so don't treat BATH as a universal rule.

quests.instruction: Which form is more typical of American English?
quests.hint: The first vowel is the difference here.
quests.explanation: American English says /ˈbeɪzəl/. British English says /ˈbæzəl/.
quests.dialectNote: Food words are good vocabulary for noticing this difference.

quests.instruction: Which form is typical of American English?
quests.hint: Pay attention to where the stress falls and the vowel in the third syllable.
quests.explanation: American /əˈrɛɡənoʊ/ is stressed on the second syllable. British /ˌɒrɪˈɡɑːnəʊ/ is stressed on the third.
quests.dialectNote: The unfamiliar stress can make the word hard to recognise.

quests.instruction: Which form is more common in British English?
quests.hint: The first vowel changes between the two versions.
quests.explanation: British English commonly uses /ˈjɒɡət/ with a short rounded vowel. American English uses /ˈjoʊɡərt/.
quests.dialectNote: Both forms are widely understood.

quests.instruction: Only one phrase is consistent with General American. Which one?
quests.hint: Look for a feature that belongs to a different accent slipping into one of the options.
quests.explanation: The first phrase has a tapped /t/ in both words. In the other phrase, the second word has a glottal stop, which is typical of British speech.
quests.dialectNote: A consistent accent uses features that go together.

quests.instruction: Which phrase is fully General American?
quests.hint: One phrase mixes an American /r/ with a British glide.
quests.explanation: The American phrase drops /j/, while the other keeps it, which is British.
quests.dialectNote: Mixed accents exist in real life, but the pattern is helpful for training.

quests.instruction: Which phrase is fully General American?
quests.hint: Look at both the vowel and the consonants.
quests.explanation: The first phrase has /ɑ/ and a tap. The second has a British vowel with an American tap.
quests.dialectNote: Speakers who blend accents are common in international workplaces.

quests.instruction: Which phrase is fully Southern British?
quests.hint: The second phrase mixes British and American features.
quests.explanation: The first has no /r/ and a long vowel in dance, both Southern British. The second keeps /r/, which is American.
quests.dialectNote: Southern British features are clustered.

quests.instruction: Which phrase is fully Southern British?
quests.hint: One option has a clear British vowel with an American consonant.
quests.explanation: The first has a clear /t/ and no final /r/. The second has an American tap.
quests.dialectNote: Look for consistency.

quests.instruction: Which phrase is fully Southern British?
quests.hint: The vowels in the first two words should match each other in the target accent.
quests.explanation: Southern British lengthens the vowel in both half and past. The other phrase uses a short vowel in 'half'.
quests.dialectNote: Learners often notice one feature and miss others.

quests.instruction: Which process explains this spoken form?
quests.hint: The first sound has been replaced by a stop, not a fricative.
quests.explanation: In th-stopping, /θ/ becomes /t/. It is characteristic of Irish English and several other varieties.
quests.dialectNote: Do not confuse it with the /f/ replacement heard in London.

quests.instruction: Which process explains this spoken form?
quests.hint: The middle consonant is now a fricative made with the lower lip.
quests.explanation: In th-fronting, /ð/ is replaced by /v/ in London-influenced English.
quests.dialectNote: This is a different process from th-stopping.

quests.instruction: Which process explains this spoken form?
quests.hint: The initial sound changed but is not missing.
quests.explanation: Here /θ/ is realised as /t/, a case of th-stopping.
quests.dialectNote: The final 'b' is silent in all varieties.

quests.instruction: Which version keeps a distinction that many Scottish speakers preserve?
quests.hint: The first sound could be breathier.
quests.explanation: Many Scottish speakers distinguish /ʍ/ in whale from /w/ in wail.
quests.dialectNote: For most English speakers, whale and wail sound the same.

quests.instruction: Which version shows the Scottish distinction?
quests.hint: Compare 'weather' and 'whether'.
quests.explanation: Speakers who keep /ʍ/ distinguish whether from weather. Others pronounce them the same.
quests.dialectNote: The distinction is receding among younger speakers.

quests.instruction: Which version reflects the /ʍ/ sound?
quests.hint: This is the same feature in an everyday adjective.
quests.explanation: Older speakers in Scotland, Ireland and some American regions distinguish white from Wight.
quests.dialectNote: Historically, English had /ʍ/ in all wh- words.

quests.instruction: Which version would come from a speaker in the English Midlands or Northwest?
quests.hint: Some accents add a hard 'g' after the nasal.
quests.explanation: In these accents the velar nasal is followed by /ɡ/, giving /ˈsɪŋɡə/.
quests.dialectNote: Some speakers in the Midlands and North West of England pronounce the /g/ after the nasal in words like singer and strong, while many others do not.

quests.instruction: Which version shows the Midlands pattern?
quests.hint: Listen at the end of the word.
quests.explanation: In some varieties a final /ɡ/ is pronounced after the nasal.
quests.dialectNote: Where this pattern occurs, it is a regional marker rather than a sign of formality.

quests.instruction: Which version shows the same regional pattern?
quests.hint: It happens inside the word too.
quests.explanation: In the same accents, the /ɡ/ is pronounced inside words like bringing.
quests.dialectNote: It is a regional marker in England.

quests.instruction: Which phrase fits traditional Boston-area speech?
quests.hint: Both words have an r before a consonant or at the end.
quests.explanation: In traditional eastern New England speech the r is not pronounced in car park.
quests.dialectNote: Boston has a distinct dialect.

quests.instruction: Which phrase is fully Southern British?
quests.hint: Combine the BATH-type vowel, the missing r and the /t/.
quests.explanation: Southern British English combines the long vowel, no r and a clear /t/.
quests.dialectNote: Try producing the phrase both ways.

quests.instruction: Which phrase is fully Southern British?
quests.hint: The first word is identical in both. Compare only the second.
quests.explanation: Southern British drops the /r/ and keeps a clear /t/ in party. The other phrase mixes in the American /r/ and tap.
quests.dialectNote: Check every sound in the phrase rather than stopping at the first clue.
